title: What is known about 1RB0LD_0RC0RF_1LD0RB_1LE---_0LA0LB_0LE0RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LD_0RC0RF_1LD0RB_1LE---_0LA0LB_0LE0RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves the two conversions the sweeps make and the situations that lead to a halt (kernel), and no halt in the first 107 steps (native_decide); the C simulator finds no halt in 109 steps.

What it does. At the left end the tape is a handful of long blocks of 1s, for example A> 000 13 00 1x 00 17 000 1y 0001000 1z. Going right, C packs every 1111 into 1000; going left, E unpacks every 0001 back into 1111. One round trip changes the counts by fixed amounts: in the example x and y lose 8 and z gains 32. When a count runs out the blocks are rearranged and a new epoch starts with larger counts (epochs begin with a block of 285, 851, 1,145 and 1,553 ones in the first 6·106 steps).

Where a halt would come from. Only D reading a 1 halts; D is entered from A reading a 1 or C reading a 0 with a 1 to the left. In 2·108 steps D always reads a 0. A proof would follow the counters through every epoch change, as for a counter machine.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 31,579 cells have been visited and 21,306 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.476). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.52).

claims.title: Shift rules
claims.text: Going right, C turns each 1111 into 1000 (ten steps a copy); going left, E with 00 ahead turns each 0001 into 1111 (28 steps a copy).

claims.title: The halting situations
claims.text: 1 A>1 and 1 C>0 halt after one step, 1 1 E>0 after two.

claims.title: Counters and epochs
claims.text: At every left-end visit with A in front of 000 in the first 107 steps, the tape is a short list of blocks of 1s; within an epoch the counts change by the same amounts every round trip (for example x − 8, y − 8, z + 32, or x − 12, y − 4, z + 32), and an epoch ends when one of them runs out.

claims.title: D never reads a 1 in 2·10<sup>8</sup> steps
claims.text: In the first 2·10<sup>8</sup> steps the machine is in state D 26,324,186 times, every time on a 0: the halting transition D1 is never close to firing in a way the run shows.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The counts behave like the registers of a counter machine; a proof needs the rules for every epoch change, and nobody has them yet.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine is a counter machine in disguise: its tape holds a few long blocks of 1s whose lengths go up and down by fixed amounts on every trip. This page runs it in your browser and shows the counters.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 31,579 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The growth shape of the two sides of the tape (see below).

sections.heading: Packing and unpacking
html: The head sweeps the whole tape. Going right, C packs each group of four 1s into 1000, ten steps a group:
Going left, E (with 0 0 ahead of it) unpacks each 0001 back into 1111, 28 steps a group:
Lean proves both for any number of groups (pack, unpack). So at the right end the tape is in the packed form (1000)n, at the left end in the unpacked form.

sections.heading: A few counters
html: Stop the simulator each time A reaches the left end. The tape is a handful of long blocks, for instance at step 2,438,703

Two blocks lost 8 ones and the last gained 32. This goes on for many trips, like the registers of a counter machine. When a block runs out, the blocks are rearranged and a new epoch starts with other increments and larger counts. Nothing so far looks close to 1 A>1 or 1 C>0, the two ways to halt.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.476). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.52).
After 109 steps the tape spans 31,579 cells (5,824 left of the start, 16,937 right), with a density of 1s of 0.675.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A counter machine in disguise: the tape is a few long blocks of 1s whose lengths change by fixed amounts on every round trip (for long stretches 8 ones leave two blocks and 32 join a third), until a block runs out and the tape is reorganised into a longer epoch. Open.
family: two-sided bouncer, words 1111 | 1000, a few counters in epochs
